source: Wurgaft, Prystawski, Gandhi, Zhang, Tenenbaum, Goodman (2025) Scaling up the think-aloud method
finding: Full pipeline: speech-to-text (Whisper), then an LLM codes each transcript as a search graph (game states as nodes). Largest think-aloud study found; the LLM coder is close to but below human-human agreement.
numbers: 640 think-aloud participants plus 60 controls on Prolific; 10 Game-of-24 trials each; 4,947 usable trials. Seven LLMs tested on 50 human-coded trials with 10 in-context examples; metric is normalized graph edit distance. All LLMs agreed significantly less with humans than humans with each other (p<0.002), but distributions overlapped, best for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, DeepSeek V3, Llama 4 Maverick.
quote: Automated coding of think-aloud data was originally proposed by Waterman & Newell (1971)
limits: One task (Game of 24), one reliability set of 50 trials, two human coders who were authors. Reliability described as moderate.
agent_relevance: A code-checked graph schema plus in-context examples is a workable way to code traces at scale; supports our rule that code, not the model, checks the coding (the checker rejects non-runnable or impossible graphs).

source: Wurgaft, Prystawski, Gandhi, Zhang, Tenenbaum, Goodman (2025) Scaling up the think-aloud method (cost and errors)
finding: Automatic coding is far cheaper than hand coding but needs a program that checks the output; some errors survive repeated auto-correction.
numbers: Humans took on average 8h15m to annotate 50 trials (about 816 h for all 4,947). Claude coded all trials in under 2 h for $74. After five rounds of automatic graph checking and correction, three error types remained (non-runnable code, wrong resulting states, operations using numbers not present); Claude 3.5 Sonnet had the fewest and never produced non-runnable code. Subgoals appeared in only 9.0% of trials (445); 58% of participants set none.
limits: Cost figures are for 2025 API prices. Rare events such as subgoals leave little data for reliability.
agent_relevance: Coding of traces can be a cheap automated pass if a validator loops errors back (mirrors G2: revise from real checker output).

source: Wurgaft, Prystawski, Gandhi, Zhang, Tenenbaum, Goodman (2025) Scaling up the think-aloud method (reactivity in their data)
finding: Asking people to think aloud did not change which problems were easy or hard, but slowed them and may have lowered accuracy slightly.
numbers: Control found the solution in 53% of trials vs 49% with think-aloud (permutation p=0.067). Response time 125.1 s vs 117.7 s (p=0.008). Problem-level accuracy split-half correlation r=0.83 within think-aloud vs r=0.79 between conditions (p=0.74). Problem-level response-time correlation across conditions r=0.95.
limits: Between-subject, 60 controls only; accuracy difference near but not at significance.
agent_relevance: Verbalizing is mostly non-reactive for humans, so human protocols are a fair gold standard; for LLMs, writing out the trace changes the computation itself, so the analogy needs care.

source: Fox, Ericsson, Best (2011) Do procedures for verbal reporting of thinking have to be reactive? A meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin)
finding: Core validity result of protocol analysis: plain think-aloud does not change performance, but explaining or describing does.
numbers: 94 studies, nearly 3,500 participants. Think-aloud effect size r=-.03 (indistinguishable from zero), nonreactive even after controlling task type (visual vs nonvisual). Procedures that ask to describe or explain thoughts were significantly reactive and raised performance over silent control. All verbal reporting tends to raise completion time.
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC; meta-analysis mixes task types; ill-structured design tasks are rarely included.
agent_relevance: Distinguish saying what you do from explaining why: a scaffold that forces explanation steps will change the solution process, not just record it (consistent with the G1 result on forced doubt).

source: Sakib, Hurst, Safayeni (2026) Evaluating the performance of large language models in taxonomic classification of questions in verbal protocols of design (AI EDAM 40)
finding: Direct test of an LLM doing protocol-analysis coding of design talk, using Eris's question taxonomy via in-context learning.
numbers: Dataset d1: 31 tutoring sessions, 2,032 question utterances from six student teams (90 for in-context learning, 1,942 test). d2: 265 questions from capstone peer design reviews (90 ICL, 175 test). Taxonomy: 3 categories and 21 subcategories (9 LLQ, 7 DRQ, 5 GDQ). Temperature 0, single pass, batches up to 50. Run time about 15 min for d1 and 1.5 min for d2.
limits: Only classifies questions that humans already extracted; single pass; proprietary models; authors ask whether reasoning models would do better.
agent_relevance: Cheap labeller for one design-protocol code class; shows coarse labels transfer, fine labels do not.

source: Sakib, Hurst, Safayeni (2026) Evaluating the performance of large language models in taxonomic classification of questions in verbal protocols of design (AI EDAM 40) (accuracy)
finding: LLMs match humans at the coarse category level but fall well short at the fine subcategory level.
numbers: Category-level alignment up to 85.7% for GPT-4.1 and 82.9% for Claude Sonnet 4.5 per the abstract; experiment 2 ranged 76.7% to 85.1%. Subcategory level: GPT-4.1 52.5% vs 74.7% human inter-rater agreement. The fetch tool noted a conflict: body text seems to give 80.2% for GPT-4.1 and 85.7% as human agreement at category level.
limits: Abstract and body disagree on the 85.7% figure; check full text before citing it.
agent_relevance: Plan on coarse codes (a handful of kinds of move) for automated trace coding; do not trust 20+ category schemes without a human audit.

source: Sakib, Hurst, Safayeni (2026) Evaluating the performance of large language models in taxonomic classification of questions in verbal protocols of design (AI EDAM 40) (prompt conditions)
finding: Prompt choices moved accuracy a lot at the extremes but little among sensible prompts; the two models were mostly statistically comparable.
numbers: Experiment 1 alignment ranged from 57.00% (no system prompt, no examples) to 80.3% (best condition G). Prompt and ICL-source differences were mostly small between reasonable configurations.
limits: Single run at temperature 0; residual non-determinism noted by authors.
agent_relevance: Giving the taxonomy and a few labeled examples is the main gain (about 23 points); further prompt tuning is minor.

source: Sakib (2024) Automating Protocol Analysis with Generative AI: Classifying Questions in Design Review Meetings Using GPT-4 (Univ. Waterloo thesis; DCC'24 paper)
finding: Earlier GPT-4 version of the same work: reasonable agreement with human labels on stand-alone questions, with generalization across datasets.
numbers: Abstract only (numbers are in the PDF, not read): factors varied were prompt data size, contextual information, prompt engineering strategy, cross-dataset use, cross-model use. Added context does not always help and can reduce performance. Claude 3.5 gave no significant drop at lower cost.
limits: Thesis abstract only; accuracy depends on dataset quality.
agent_relevance: More context in the coding prompt can hurt: give the coder the single unit plus the codebook, not the whole transcript.

source: Kelly & Gero (2025) Semantic and network analysis of design protocols to reveal design framing phenomena (ICED25, Proc. Design Society 5)
finding: Gero's group now uses gpt-4o to extract concepts from design think-aloud, then builds semantic networks to spot framing; they admit the LLM step is unreliable.
numbers: 17 participants, two problems (coffee cup, bike rack), 16-minute sessions split into 2-second segments to match fMRI timing. gpt-4o-2024-08-06 coded concepts; text-embedding-3-small embeddings weighted 0.8 concept + 0.2 sentence; k-means up to 50 clusters. Degree-to-connectivity correlations 0.721 (bike to coffee) and 0.710 (coffee to bike). Designer P9 global similarity fell below 0.5 on 30 (coffee) and 35 (bike) occasions vs 12 and 16 for P3.
quote: Using an LLM for identifying concepts is inherently unreliable, both internally
limits: Small N; no human reliability benchmark reported; the paper itself calls LLM concept identification unreliable internally and against humans.
agent_relevance: Shows the design-cognition field moving from FBS hand-coding toward LLM plus embeddings; any trace analysis we do must report repeat-run agreement of the coder.

source: Lee, Jin, Hyun (2026) Beyond Semantic Similarity: Open Challenges for Embedding-Based Creative Process Analysis Across AI Design Tools
finding: Position paper: fuzzy linkography (embedding similarity between design moves) can miss creative pivots hidden inside similar wording, and becomes circular when embeddings steer an agent.
numbers: No quantitative results (4-page paper). Three open challenges: aligning similarity with creative significance, segmenting multimodal traces, and agentic systems where embedding metrics enter the generation loop. Example: two moves both mention stackable modules but address different problems yet score as similar.
limits: Position paper, no experiments.
agent_relevance: Linkography-style metrics on our own traces will mistake a reframe for elaboration; use a code-detected change of the stated problem as the pivot signal rather than text similarity.

source: Tajik et al. (2026) Disagreement as Data: Reasoning Trace Analytics in Multi-Agent Systems (LAK26)
finding: Treats LLM reasoning traces from coding agents as process data: similarity of two agents' reasoning separates agreement from disagreement and flags ambiguous codes.
numbers: 9,746 agent-agent pairs coding human tutoring dialogue segments; DeepSeek-R1 agents, BERT embeddings, cosine similarity. Agreement pairs mean cosine 0.957 (SD 0.025) vs disagreement 0.904 (SD 0.058); Welch t(9746)=60.33, p<.001, Cohen's d=1.16. Correlation between cosine and label agreement 0.54 (95% CI .52-.55).
limits: One tutoring codebook; BERT truncated at 512 tokens; cosine tracks surface wording.
agent_relevance: Disagreement between two coders' reasoning is usable as a trigger for human review, matching G1 (act on a signal) and G4 (agreement is a hint).

source: Tajik et al. (2026) Disagreement as Data: Reasoning Trace Analytics in Multi-Agent Systems (LAK26) (four-way split)
finding: Label agreement and reasoning agreement come apart in a minority of cases, which exposes fuzzy code boundaries.
numbers: Within-align (same label, similar reasoning) 47.0%, N=4,598, mean cosine 0.965. Between-misalign (different labels and reasoning) 28.0%, N=2,680, cosine 0.863 (table lists 23.0%). Within-misalign (same label, different reasoning) N=2,193, cosine 0.916. Between-align (different labels, similar reasoning) 275 pairs, cosine 0.954. Codes such as Aligning to Prior Knowledge and Guiding Feedback had low human kappa (about 0.6-0.66).
limits: Share figures are inconsistent in the extracted text (23% vs 3% vs 28%); counts N are more reliable.
agent_relevance: Same label for different reasons suggests the label is too coarse; log the reason with each code in trace analysis.

source: Dunivin (2024) Scalable Qualitative Coding with LLMs: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Matches Human Performance in Some Hermeneutic Tasks
finding: Asking the model for a rationale before the code raises agreement with a human gold standard.
numbers: 232 NYT passages on W.E.B. Du Bois (111 gold), 9 codes, zero-shot, temp 0. GPT-4 per-code mean Cohen's kappa 0.676 with rationale vs 0.592 without; full-codebook-in-one-prompt 0.596 vs 0.465. GPT-3.5 per-code 0.338 with rationale vs 0.291 without. Abstract: kappa >=0.6 on 8 of 9 codes (a recount from the table gives 7). Worst code Out of the Mouth of Activists kappa 0.304 (n=11).
limits: One topic, one gold standard, codebook revised using model rationales; small codes unstable.
agent_relevance: Coding one code per call with a short stated reason beats one big call; note this is the coder's reasoning, not the solver's.

source: Dunivin (2024) Scalable Qualitative Coding with LLMs: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Matches Human Performance in Some Hermeneutic Tasks (per-code detail)
finding: Chain-of-thought gains are largest for rare or hard codes; model size matters.
numbers: Per-code GPT-4 kappa with vs without rationale: Coalition Building 0.597 vs 0.444; Out of the Mouth of Activists 0.304 vs 0.092; Monumental Memorialization 1.000 vs 0.913; Scholar 0.609 vs 0.516. Per-code prompting beats full codebook (0.68 vs 0.60).
limits: Small n for several codes.
agent_relevance: Split a multi-code protocol scheme into separate yes/no coder calls.

source: QualiGPT authors (2024) When Qualitative Research Meets Large Language Model: Exploring the Potential of QualiGPT
finding: GPT-4 deductive coding reaches only moderate agreement with humans, yet is very stable run to run.
numbers: Human-human Cohen's kappa 0.73. GPT-4 vs humans Fleiss kappa 0.44-0.50 (mean about 0.46). Three GPT-4 runs vs each other 0.87. GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 vs humans 0.38-0.42. With 50 agreed examples as prior knowledge on 150 more entries: LLM-human 0.46, while the two human assistants fell to 0.64. Inductive coding Cohen's kappa 0.57.
limits: Data are interview-style qualitative data, not think-aloud.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run stability (0.87) exceeds agreement with humans (0.46): the coder is consistent but differs from humans, so repeated sampling does not fix coding bias (G4).

source: Kirsten, Buckmann, Mhaidli, Becker (2024) Decoding Complexity: Exploring Human-AI Concordance in Qualitative Coding
finding: Agreement with humans falls as the coding task becomes more interpretive, for humans and models alike.
numbers: Three tasks A-C of rising interpretive depth on interview data, Cohen's kappa. Humans: almost perfect on A and B, substantial on C. GPT-4: almost perfect on A in all settings; moderate to substantial on B; moderate on C in all settings. GPT-3.5: fair on C for one-shot and few-shot. GPT-4 beat GPT-3.5 in all three tasks. Inter-human agreement was generally higher than model-human.
limits: Exact kappa table not extracted; synthetic interview data for examples.
agent_relevance: Expect LLM coding of interpretive design moves (reframing, intent) to be the weakest; start with surface moves.

source: Journal of Learning Analytics (2026) Using Large Language Models for Automated Coding of Self-Regulated Learning Think-Aloud Protocol Data
finding: Closest published test of LLMs coding true concurrent think-aloud transcripts: accuracy depends on task, code and model.
numbers: 600 utterances (300 per task), math vs biology; GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro; six prompt conditions; accuracy from .49 to .90. Math M=.78, significantly above biology. Claude M=.71, GPT-4o M=.69 (Claude vs GPT-4o OR=0.81, p=.016), Gemini lower. Highest code MPS M=.73.
limits: Binary present/absent coding per code; accuracy not kappa; only STEM tasks.
agent_relevance: Metacognitive monitoring codes are the unstable ones; coding monitoring behaviour in agent traces will be less reliable than coding operators.

source: Journal of Learning Analytics (2026) Using Large Language Models for Automated Coding of Self-Regulated Learning Think-Aloud Protocol Data (prompt effects, human reliability)
finding: Few-shot examples helped one code and hurt another; added context did nothing.
numbers: Human coders: kappa 0.65 (math, 74.0% agreement) and 0.66 (biology, 79.2%); positive agreement 0.65-0.67, negative agreement 0.998; 3,800 math and 6,591 biology verbalizations coded by humans. Few-shot vs zero-shot overall OR=0.90 (p=.111, n.s.). Sub-goal setting: zero-shot 81.6% vs few-shot 71.2% (OR=0.56, p_adj<.001). Negative judgment of learning: few-shot 90.1% vs 85.9% (p_adj=.054). Context (none, task-aligned, course-aligned) no significant effect (task-aligned OR=0.88, p=.102).
limits: Human kappa itself only about 0.65; positive agreement is moderate.
agent_relevance: Per-code testing needed: a prompt trick that helps one code can hurt another; check each code against a human sample before trusting it.

source: Marjanovic, Patel et al. (2026) DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology: Let's think about LLM reasoning (TMLR)
finding: Applies protocol-analysis style segmentation to reasoning chains: a human-process taxonomy mapped onto the chain, with a model-specific cycle structure.
numbers: Human stages (problem definition, initial response, planning, execution and monitoring, reconstruction, verification) drawn from Polya and others; R1 chain becomes Problem definition, Bloom cycle, Reconstruction cycles, Final decision. 400 chains annotated by GPT-4o prompted with hand-written rules and human few-shot examples, 100 per task (math, context faithfulness, psycholinguistic stimuli, harmful QA); authors inspected the annotations.
limits: Annotation validated by author inspection; no formal kappa in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Reusable pass for labelling our own traces; note R1 plans as it executes, with no separate planning stage, unlike human protocols.

source: Marjanovic, Patel et al. (2026) DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology: Let's think about LLM reasoning (TMLR) (rumination and sweet spot)
finding: R1 repeatedly re-examines ideas it already checked (rumination), which does not work as faithful self-monitoring; there is a reasoning-length sweet spot.
numbers: Rumination measured as n-gram repetition rate; it rises with problem difficulty. Accuracy vs thought length rises, peaks, then falls on AIME-24 (normalised bins). Multiplication: always right up to 6x6 digits, almost always wrong above 12x12, rise-then-fall only for 7x7 to 11x11.
quote: does not indicate faithful process monitoring
limits: Single model (R1); taxonomy hand-built.
agent_relevance: Supports G1: doubt without a signal wastes tokens and can lower accuracy; count repeated n-grams in code as a stall signal.

source: Gandhi, Chakravarthy et al. (2025) Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners (COLM 2025)
finding: Codes four human problem-solving behaviours (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) in model traces with an LLM classifier, and shows they predict which model improves under RL.
numbers: Countdown task: Qwen-2.5-3B reaches about 60% after RL while Llama-3.2-3B stays near 30%; Qwen shows the behaviours naturally. Priming Llama with traces containing the behaviours lets it match Qwen. Priming with empty chain-of-thought gave 30-35%, about the base level. Priming on incorrect solutions with the right behaviours matched priming on correct ones.
limits: Training-time result, 3B models, Countdown mainly.
agent_relevance: Protocol-style behaviour codes (verify, backtrack, subgoal, work backward) are a validated vocabulary for LLM traces and can be counted by code.

source: Gandhi, Chakravarthy et al. (2025) Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners (COLM 2025) (coder reliability)
finding: GPT-4o-mini counting of behaviours agrees substantially with humans on most codes, poorly on one.
numbers: 100 random trajectories; ICC3 of GPT-4o-mini vs two humans: verification 0.66 and 0.65 (vs Claude 0.70); backtracking 0.67 (vs Claude 0.74); subgoal setting 0.70 and 0.77 (vs Claude 0.88); backward chaining 0.55 and 0.40 (vs Claude 0.78). Classifier asked 4 questions per trajectory at temperature 0, 512 tokens, with examples of each behaviour.
limits: Two human raters; LLM-LLM agreement exceeds LLM-human agreement, which suggests shared bias.
agent_relevance: Cheap and reliable enough for verify, backtrack and subgoal; do not use LLM-only coding for backward chaining.

source: Bogdan, Macar, Nanda, Conmy (2025) Thought Anchors: Which LLM reasoning steps matter?
finding: Sentence-level coding of reasoning traces plus counterfactual resampling shows which kinds of sentence steer the answer.
numbers: Eight sentence categories (problem setup, plan generation, fact retrieval, active computation, uncertainty management, result consolidation, self checking, final answer) labelled by GPT-4o. Plan generation and uncertainty management sentences have the highest counterfactual importance; fact retrieval and active computation lower. Forced-answer importance under-rates planning.
limits: Reasoning-model distills; math tasks; labeller accuracy not quantified in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Coded plan and doubt moves are causally load-bearing, so coding them is worth it; counterfactual resampling is a code-side test of whether a coded step mattered.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Core threat to protocol analysis of models: the written trace often omits the factor that drove the answer.
numbers: Faithfulness scores overall 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (DeepSeek R1); on misalignment hints 20% and 29%. Models verbalize used hints at least 1% of the time in most settings, often under 20%. Unfaithful traces were longer, not shorter; harder tasks less faithful (44% relative drop for Claude, 32% for R1 on GPQA vs MMLU). Reward hacks verbalized in under 2% of examples in 5 of 6 RL environments.
limits: Hints in prompts, single forward-pass reasoning; Baker et al. (2025) found over 90% detection for coding reward hacks.
agent_relevance: Ericsson-Simon validity assumes verbalization reflects heeded information; for LLMs it often does not, so G2 (cite code-found output, not the model's story) is justified.

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Early demonstration that chain-of-thought explanations can be systematically unfaithful.
numbers: Biasing features (reordered answer options, suggested answer) drop accuracy by as much as 36% on a suite of 13 tasks while the CoT never mentions the bias; models alter explanations to justify the biased answer.
limits: Older models; biasing prompts.
agent_relevance: Reading the trace as a faithful record is unsafe; analyse behaviour (what changed, which checks ran) over stated reasons.

source: Kim, Kim, Son, Yang, Kim (2026) What Did the AI Take On? Characterizing Cognitive Delegation in LLM Reasoning
finding: Retrospective human annotation of LLM reasoning steps (a retrospective-report variant of protocol analysis) shows users see about half the steps as AI-initiated.
numbers: 24 participants, three knowledge-work tasks, 992 retrospective annotations of reasoning steps. 48.6% of steps judged AI-initiated, rising from 31.1% in the first fifth of a turn to 61.4% in the final fifth. 62.7% of AI-initiated steps contributed as intended; users preferred full delegation for 63.9% of steps but wanted involvement in 28% of critical steps.
limits: Retrospective (not concurrent) reports; one model; small sample.
agent_relevance: Human review of traces should target critical steps, not all steps; supports sparse human gates.

source: Li, Mo, Tang et al. (2026) HugAgent: A Human Simulation Benchmark for Individual-Level Reasoning
finding: Uses human think-aloud interviews as gold reasoning traces; models infer a person's belief state fairly well but predict belief updates poorly.
numbers: Belief state inference accuracy about 71.1% and belief dynamics update about 66.2% in one headline condition; cross-domain belief-dynamics accuracy falls from 62.25% to 24.84%; context variants move accuracy from 58.49% to 74.66% (state) and 39.83% to 63.11% (dynamics).
limits: Self-reported belief reasoning in three policy domains, not design tasks; several figures read from partial text.
agent_relevance: Think-aloud as ground truth for how a mind updates remains a hard target for LLMs; model-simulated protocols are not human protocols.

source: UXCascade authors (2026) UXCascade: Scalable Usability Testing with Simulated User Agents
finding: A tool in which LLM user-agents produce think-aloud style logs (prompt: think aloud in first person at each observation) that UX experts then review.
numbers: Qualitative system paper; agents emit first-person think-aloud traces plus action logs; experts asked for think-aloud as a model for reading agent runs. Related UXAgent simulates think-aloud. No accuracy against real human think-aloud was found in the text read.
limits: Only matching passages skimmed; no human-protocol validation number found.
agent_relevance: Method already inside an agent loop: prompt an agent to narrate each step, then analyse the narration; but the narration is generated, not a protocol of an independent process.

source: Waterman & Newell (1971) Protocol analysis as a task for artificial intelligence (PAS-II)
finding: Earliest attempt to automate protocol analysis, cited by Wurgaft et al. as the original proposal; limited by 1971 AI.
numbers: No numbers read; known only through Wurgaft et al. (2025).
limits: Not opened; secondhand.
agent_relevance: The idea of a program that turns verbal reports into a problem-behaviour graph is 50 years old; the new part is a coder that handles free text.
